issues.legal_issue: A legislature may authorize the executive to withdraw a statutory exemption without impermissibly delegating essential legislative functions when the statute itself establishes the governing policy.
material_facts: The land-reform statute exempted land used for linaloe cultivation, but made that exemption subject to a provision authorizing the State Government to withdraw exemptions by notification.
The statute restricted the extent of land that could be acquired for linaloe cultivation and separately prohibited companies from holding agricultural land.
The challenged statute formed part of a broader land-reform scheme addressing landholding, transfers, and exemptions.
issues.conclusion: The provision authorizing withdrawal of the exemption was valid and did not involve excessive delegation of legislative power.
issues.legal_principle: Under In re Delhi Laws Act, 1912, legislative power may be delegated for implementation of legislative policy, but essential legislative functions may not be surrendered. Whether a delegation is excessive depends on the statute’s subject matter, scheme, provisions, preamble, and context; the court considers the enactment as a whole. Maharashtra State Board of Secondary and Higher Secondary Education v. Paritosh Bhupeshkumar Sheth; Bhatnagars & Co. Ltd. v. Union of India; and Mohmedalli v. Union of India were also relied on. The court read the exemption as conditional because the provision granting it was expressly made subject to the withdrawal provision.

predicates.delegation_validity_challenge: A person challenging a delegated power alleges that the legislature transferred essential policy-making authority to the executive.
predicates.statutory_exemption_is_conditional: The legislature made an exemption subject to a provision allowing the executive to withdraw it.
predicates.legislative_policy_is_discernible: The statutory scheme and related restrictions disclose the policy governing the exemption and its withdrawal.

issues.definition: When a challenged delegated power concerns withdrawal of a conditional exemption and the statute discloses the governing policy, the power is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Failure to lay a published notification before the legislature does not invalidate it when the laying requirement does not make prior legislative approval a condition of its effectiveness.
material_facts: The State Government issued and published a notification withdrawing the exemption.
The notification had not initially been laid before the State Legislature.
The laying provision allowed the Houses to modify or annul a notification after it was laid, and the Court directed that it be placed before both Houses.
issues.conclusion: The failure to lay the notification did not invalidate it or the action taken under it, and the defect was curable.
issues.legal_principle: The effect of a laying clause depends on its wording and the degree of legislative control it establishes. In Jan Mohammad Noor Mohammad Bagban v. State of Gujarat, failure to lay rules did not invalidate them. Atlas Cycle Industries Ltd. v. State of Haryana held that non-compliance with a laying clause did not invalidate an order. Quarry Owners’ Association v. State of Bihar held that an omission to lay a notification did not affect its validity and could be addressed by later placement before the legislature.

predicates.notification_validity_challenge: A person challenges a notification on the ground that it was not placed before the legislature.
predicates.notification_was_published: The executive published the notification in the official gazette.
predicates.laying_clause_allows_later_legislative_m: The laying procedure permits the legislature to modify or annul the notification after it has been placed before it.

issues.definition: If a published notification is challenged for non-laying and the legislature can modify or annul it after placement, non-laying does not invalidate the notification.

issues.legal_issue: A general delegated legislative measure withdrawing an exemption does not require an individual hearing or reasons unless the governing law requires them.
material_facts: The exemption was withdrawn by a notification made under delegated statutory authority.
The statute contained no requirement to provide an affected person a hearing or to record reasons before withdrawing the exemption.
issues.conclusion: A hearing and recorded reasons were not preconditions to withdrawing the exemption by notification.
issues.legal_principle: Delegated legislation is legislative in character. In the absence of a statutory requirement, the principles of natural justice do not require a hearing before such legislation is made, and the legislature or its delegate need not give reasons while discharging a legislative function. The court relied on State of Punjab v. Tehal Singh; West Bengal Electricity Regulatory Commission v. CESC Ltd.; Pune Municipal Corporation v. Promoters and Builders Association; and Bihar State Electricity Board v. Pulak Enterprises.

predicates.challenge_to_general_legislative_measure: An affected person challenges a general measure made through legislative or delegated legislative authority.
predicates.measure_withdraws_exemption: The measure withdraws an exemption previously available under the statutory scheme.
predicates.no_hearing_or_reasons_requirement: The governing law does not require an individual hearing or recorded reasons before the measure is made.

issues.definition: When a general legislative measure withdraws an exemption and the law requires neither a hearing nor reasons, neither is a precondition to making the measure.

issues.legal_issue: A company cannot rely on an exemption that has been withdrawn to hold agricultural land when the governing land-reform scheme bars companies from holding such land.
material_facts: A company acquired land used for linaloe cultivation while that use was exempt from the land-reform provisions.
The exemption was conditional and was later withdrawn by notification.
The statutory scheme prohibited companies from holding agricultural land and restricted transfers to persons disentitled to hold it.
issues.conclusion: After withdrawal of the exemption, the land was governed by the land-reform provisions, and the company could not rely on the former exemption to hold it.
issues.legal_principle: The court applied the provisions governing companies’ landholding, transfers to persons disentitled from holding land, conditional exemptions, and withdrawal of exemptions: Sections 79B, 80, 107, and 110 of the Karnataka Land Reforms Act. It held that the purchaser took the land subject to the statutory condition attached to the exemption. The land-reform provisions were protected by Article 31B because they had been included in the Ninth Schedule.

predicates.corporate_purchaser_holds_agricultural_l: A company acquired and holds land that is agricultural land when the statutory exemption does not apply.
predicates.exemption_has_been_withdrawn: The executive withdrew the exemption that had covered the land’s use.
predicates.corporate_landholding_is_barred: The governing landholding scheme prohibits a company from holding the relevant agricultural land.

issues.definition: A company that holds agricultural land cannot rely on an exemption for that land after the exemption is withdrawn if the landholding scheme bars the company from holding it.

issues.legal_issue: A state acquisition law whose dominant purpose is agrarian reform and protection of an estate is protected by the constitutional provision governing acquisition of estates, even if it includes ancillary measures concerning associated valuables.
material_facts: The acquisition law provided for acquisition and management of an estate containing land used for linaloe cultivation and its tree growth.
The stated purposes included preserving the estate and its valuable objects and establishing an art gallery and museum.
The State Legislature passed the law, and the President assented to it.
The court found that preserving and protecting the estate was the law’s dominant purpose and that measures concerning paintings and other valuables were ancillary.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition law was protected by Article 31A(1)(a) and was immune from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31A(1)(a), read with Article 31A(2)(a)(iii), protects laws directed to acquisition of estates and agrarian reform. Whether a law concerns agrarian reform is determined by its substance and dominant purpose, not merely its outward form; ancillary provisions do not remove the protection. The court relied on State of Kerala v. Gwalior Rayon Silk Manufacturing (Wvg.) Co.; Kunjukutty Sahib v. State of Kerala; and Mahant Sankarshan Ramanuja Das Goswami v. State of Orissa.

rule.if: constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_law and dominant_purpose_is_agrarian_reform and ancillary_measures_support_that_purpose and required_presidential_assent_was_obtained

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_acquisition_: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law providing for acquisition of an estate.
predicates.dominant_purpose_is_agrarian_reform: The law’s primary purpose is to preserve, protect, or reorganize land as part of agrarian reform.
predicates.ancillary_measures_support_that_purpose: The law includes additional measures that support, rather than displace, its primary land-related purpose.
predicates.required_presidential_assent_was_obtaine: The law received presidential assent where the constitutional protection required it.

issues.definition: An acquisition law with an agrarian-reform purpose, related ancillary measures, and required assent receives protection from equality and freedom challenges.

issues.legal_issue: A state acquisition law is not repugnant to central acquisition legislation merely because both concern acquisition when their dominant purposes differ and they do not occupy the same field incompatibly.
material_facts: The challenged state law primarily sought to preserve and protect an estate governed by land-reform legislation.
The central land-acquisition law concerned acquiring land for public purposes and determining compensation.
The state law also dealt incidentally with acquisition of paintings, artefacts, and other valuables.
The court found the dominant purposes and fields of the two laws materially different.
issues.conclusion: There was no repugnancy between the state law and the central land-acquisition law, and assent under Article 254(2) was not required on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Article 254 applies when state and central laws concern substantially the same subject matter and are fully inconsistent or irreconcilable so that they cannot operate together. The court examined the dominant intention and field of each law. It relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh; Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. State of Bihar; M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India; and Vijay Kumar Sharma v. State of Karnataka.

predicates.repugnancy_challenge_to_state_law: A person challenges a state law as repugnant to a central law.
predicates.state_and_central_laws_have_different_do: The state and central laws principally pursue different legislative purposes.
predicates.laws_are_not_irreconcilably_inconsistent: The laws do not create an unavoidable conflict when applied to the same facts.

issues.definition: A challenged state law is not invalid for repugnancy if its dominant purpose differs from the central law’s and the two laws are not irreconcilably inconsistent.

issues.legal_issue: Deprivation of property under Article 300A requires a public purpose and is subject to judicial review of the legal authority and the justification for no, nil, or illusory compensation.
material_facts: The acquisition law deprived owners and other interested persons of property for the stated purposes of preserving and managing an estate and establishing a gallery and museum.
The law provided for an amount to be distributed among legitimate claimants, and an amendment clarified payment to owners and interested persons.
The appellants argued that the law failed to provide adequate compensation and was expropriatory.
The Court dismissed the appeals while holding that the State must justify the public purpose and the treatment of compensation on judicially reviewable grounds.
issues.conclusion: Public purpose is a precondition to deprivation under Article 300A, and a right to claim compensation is inbuilt in that Article; the State must justify no or nil compensation on judicially reviewable standards. The appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 300A requires deprivation to be by authority of law and does not incorporate a general entitlement to a particular amount of compensation. Public purpose is a precondition. No compensation cannot be prescribed for an acquisition for public purpose, while a nil amount may be permissible in appropriate circumstances, including where the State discharges liabilities attached to the property, subject to judicial review. The law must not impose an arbitrary, excessive, or disproportionate restriction and must comply with other constitutional requirements. Article 300A does not import a compensation right from Entry 42 of List III. The court considered Jilubhai Nanbhai Khachar v. State of Gujarat; I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu; State of A.P. v. McDowell & Co.; Union of India v. G. Ganayutham; and Ashok Kumar Thakur v. Union of India, among others.

rule.if: property_deprivation_challenge and deprivation_is_authorized_by_law and primarily_public_purpose and compensation_basis_is_justifiable

predicates.property_deprivation_challenge: A person challenges a law that deprives them of property.
predicates.deprivation_is_authorized_by_law: A competent legislature has authorized the deprivation through law and the law’s requirements have been followed.
predicates.primarily_public_purpose: The property is taken primarily for a public purpose rather than primarily for private interest.
predicates.compensation_basis_is_justifiable: The law provides compensation or the State justifies nil or no compensation on judicially reviewable grounds.

issues.definition: A property deprivation may withstand constitutional review when it is authorized by law, serves a primarily public purpose, and its compensation basis is justifiable.

issues.legal_issue: Land acquired under a law for a stated purpose must be used only for that purpose.
material_facts: The estate was acquired for specified purposes that included preserving and managing the estate and establishing an art gallery and museum.
The Court dismissed the appeals and expressly directed that the acquired land be used only for the purpose for which it was acquired.
issues.conclusion: The acquired land must be used only for the purpose for which it was acquired.
issues.legal_principle: The Court imposed a purpose-limitation in its final order, requiring the acquired land to be used consistently with the purpose supporting the acquisition.

predicates.land_was_acquired_for_a_specific_purpose: The acquiring authority took land for an identified purpose.
predicates.acquisition_appeal_has_been_disposed: A court has disposed of a challenge concerning the acquisition.

issues.definition: When land has been acquired for an identified purpose and the acquisition challenge is disposed of, the land must be used only for that purpose.
